# src/lease.ts — cross-process write-ownership lock (excerpt)

> Cross-process write-ownership lock for one session's artifact directory,
> held for the whole life of a write handle. The arbiter is the kernel:
> POSIX takes a non-blocking `flock(2)` (through fs-ext) on `session.lock`
> beside the log, and **Windows holds a named kernel semaphore derived from
> that path — never a file lock or handle**, so readers, searches, and
> directory removal proceed freely while the lock is held. …

```ts
import { flock } from 'fs-ext'
import { acquireLockHandleWin32, releaseLockHandleWin32 } from './win32.ts'
```

> … **Windows has no lock file at all.** Readers never touch the lock. …

Note: `flock` is imported statically at module top — the package loader must
resolve and load `fs-ext` even on Windows, where the `flock` branch is never
taken.

references.text:
### DSH-0.1.3-A1-03 · Windows install fails on the `fs-ext` native build; the runtime never calls `flock` on Windows

- **Type**: breaking
- **Applies to**: profile wrappers / packaging; any Windows machine without Visual Studio
  Build Tools upgrading to 0.1.3-alpha.1
- **Touchpoints**: none (packaging/install surface)
- **Action level**: required-if-hit
- **Symptoms**: `pnpm install` exits 1. `fs-ext@2.1.1` runs its `node-gyp configure build`
  install script and fails with `gyp ERR! find VS … You need to install the latest version of
  Visual Studio (including the "Desktop development with C++" workload)`. `fs-ext` is a pinned
  dependency of `@deepseek-ai/dsh-session-persistence-jsonl` and is statically imported from
  `src/lease.ts`, so `pnpm install --ignore-scripts` cannot skip it — the module must exist
  and load.
- **Migration recipe**:
  1. Confirm the platform path first: on Windows, `lease.ts` takes `acquireLockHandleWin32`
     (a named kernel semaphore via `CreateSemaphoreW`) and holds "never a file lock or
     handle"; `flock` is only the POSIX branch. The native module is dead code on Windows.
  2. Add a pnpm patch (the repository already patches native packages this way, e.g.
     `patches/node-pty@*`): rewrite the install script to run `node-gyp` only on non-Windows,
     and give the entry a pure-JS `flock` fallback (warn once, no-op). Linux/macOS keep the
     native build.
  3. Register the patch in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` (`patchedDependencies` and `allowBuilds`)
     and re-run `pnpm install`.
  Do not install Visual Studio just for this, do not patch upstream, and do not rely on
  `--ignore-scripts` alone.
- **Verification**: `pnpm install` completes; `require('fs-ext')` loads and the flock callback
  path warns once instead of throwing; `dsh web --no-open` boots and answers HTTP 200.
- **Source**: [dsh-v0.1.3-alpha.1](https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness/tree/dsh-v0.1.3-alpha.1)
  (`d347e70`): `packages/session/session-persistence-jsonl/package.json` pins `"fs-ext": "2.1.1"`;
  `src/lease.ts` statically imports `flock` from `fs-ext` and routes Windows through
  `acquireLockHandleWin32`; `src/win32.ts` carries the named-semaphore bindings ·
  single-host field report (Windows 11 without MSVC, 2026-09-07)

candidate_reports.S20-msvc-flock-trap/report.md:
# S20 Diagnosis Report — Windows Install Blocker: fs-ext native build

## 1. What exactly fails, and why

- **Package**: `@deepseek-ai/dsh-session-persistence-jsonl@0.1.3-alpha.1` declares
  `"fs-ext": "2.1.1"` as a runtime dependency (fixture/manifest-excerpt.json:4-6).
- **Failing step**: during `pnpm install`, `fs-ext@2.1.1`'s install script runs
  `node-gyp configure build` (fixture/install-error.log:3).
- **Root cause**: node-gyp cannot find a C++ toolchain — `find VS` fails:
  `VCINSTALLDIR not set`, no VS installation found (fixture/install-error.log:4-11).
  The machine has **no Visual Studio / Build Tools** (no `vswhere.exe`, no VS
  directory) — fixture/README.md:3-4. So the native module `fs-ext` fails to
  compile and `pnpm install` exits 1 (fixture/install-error.log:11-14).

## 2. Why `pnpm install --ignore-scripts` cannot fix this

`--ignore-scripts` only skips running the install script at install time; it does
not provide a prebuilt binary for `fs-ext`. As a result, `fs-ext`'s native
binding (`fs_ext.node`) is never built and is missing from the package. Worse,
fixture/lease-excerpt.md:17-19 notes that `flock` is **statically imported at
module top** (`import { flock } from 'fs-ext'`), so the loader resolves and
loads `fs-ext` at import time — even on Windows, where the `flock` branch is
never taken. So with `--ignore-scripts` the install "succeeds" but the service
crashes at boot when `session-persistence-jsonl` loads `lease.ts` and hits the
unbuilt/missing `fs-ext` native addon. The failure moves from install time to
runtime; it is not fixed.

## 3. Which lock path Windows actually takes, and what that implies

From fixture/lease-excerpt.md:5-8,15-16 and fixture/win32-excerpt.ts:23-24:

- On POSIX, the write-lock is a non-blocking `flock(2)` on `session.lock`,
  provided by `fs-ext`.
- On Windows, the lock is a **named kernel semaphore** derived from the path,
  implemented in `src/win32.ts` via `CreateSemaphoreW` / `WaitForSingleObject` /
  `ReleaseSemaphore` (durable-namespace primitives `MoveFileExW`, etc.).
  There is **no lock file and no `flock(2)` call on Windows**; `flock` from
  `fs-ext` is dead code at runtime on win32.

Implication: on Windows the `fs-ext` native module is **never actually called**
— no `flock` call, nothing from its bindings is exercised. The only
problem is (a) its install-time `node-gyp` build requiring MSVC, and (b) the
static top-level import forcing the loader to load `fs-ext` even on Windows.
So `fs-ext` can be safely neutralized on Windows without changing runtime
behavior — it does not need to be compiled at all.

## 4. Concrete, least-invasive fix plan (no Visual Studio, no upstream edits)

Follow the repository's existing patch precedent
(`patches/node-pty@*.patch`, registered via `pnpm-workspace.yaml` —
fixture/README.md:7-11):

1. Create a pnpm patch for `fs-ext@2.1.1` the same way
   (`pnpm patch fs-ext@2.1.1`), producing `patches/fs-ext@2.1.1.patch`.
2. In the patched package:
   a. Replace the `install` script in `package.json` with a no-op
      (`"install": "node -e \"\""` or simply empty), so `node-gyp configure
      build` never runs — no MSVC needed.
   b. Replace the JS entry file (the module's main) with a stub that exports
      the surface the static import touches — at minimum `flock` (and any other
      named exports `lease.ts` references) — implemented as functions that
      throw only if actually invoked on win32 (they are never invoked, per
      §3), or that delegate to POSIX semantics where appropriate. Because
      Windows never calls them, the stub is runtime-inert on win32.
3. Register the patch in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` under
   `patchedDependencies:` (`"fs-ext@2.1.1": "patches/fs-ext@2.1.1.patch"`),
   alongside the existing node-pty entry.
4. Optionally, in `src/lease.ts`, convert the static
   `import { flock } from 'fs-ext'` to a dynamic/platform-gated import
   (`process.platform === 'win32' ? /* win32 path */ : require('fs-ext')`)
   so the win32 bootstrap never loads `fs-ext` at all. This is a local
   source change, not an upstream dependency change, and removes even the
   load-time resolution of the stub. (Keep the top-level import removal
   minimal; the stub already makes loading safe, so this is hardening.)
5. Run `pnpm install` on the target machine: no `node-gyp` step, no VS
   lookup, install completes. Boot the service: on Windows the win32
   named-semaphore lock path in `src/win32.ts` is used; the `fs-ext` stub
   is loaded (or skipped entirely with step 4) but never executed. Locking,
   readers, search, and directory removal semantics are unchanged.

This touches only local patch files, `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, and optionally
`src/lease.ts` — no Visual Studio install, no edits to upstream packages,
no `--ignore-scripts` hack.

## 5. Corridor card

The finding is covered by corridor card `DSH-0.1.3-A1` (the S20 / msvc-flock-trap cell of the dsh 0.1.3 upgrade corridor).

## Limitations

No external documentation was consulted; the full card id suffix after
`DSH-0.1.3-A1` could not be confirmed from the fixture materials alone.
Everything above is derived solely from the fixture evidence.
